item.text: {"question_id":"6B.6","answer":"During 2023, Lula’s government mounted targeted crisis responses, most clearly in the Yanomami emergency: it reported more than 30,000 health consultations, reopened seven posts, deployed 765 health professionals, delivered medicines, malaria tests and food, and created a malaria-control plan with active case-finding and increased testing (BATCH-0013-E004; BATCH-0013-E005; BATCH-0013-E006). The government also created a primary-care immunization coordination unit in response to low vaccination coverage and the risk of reintroduced disease (BATCH-0016-E015), and continued relocating more than 100,000 Venezuelan refugees to relieve pressure on Roraima and improve access to education and work, although post-relocation outcomes are not shown (BATCH-0001-E034). These actions demonstrate implementation directed at vulnerable populations, but the evidence does not establish broad reductions in avoidable suffering. Severe malnutrition and malaria remained, some miners returned, and Indigenous organizations documented 1,040 deaths among Indigenous children aged 0–4, including deaths from pneumonia, diarrhea and malnutrition considered avoidable through adequate care, alongside shortages of health infrastructure, personnel, transport, sanitation and water (BATCH-0013-E005; BATCH-0001-E029; BATCH-0005-E027). National food insecurity also remained extensive: more than 70 million people experienced food insecurity and 21.1 million hunger, while the government’s Brasil Sem Fome targets were not yet outcomes (BATCH-0001-E020). Vaccination coverage had been declining since 2016, and the TCU identified monitoring and program-design weaknesses, without evidence that its recommendations were implemented during 2023 (BATCH-0005-E002). Overall, the record supports responsive, partly targeted crisis administration, especially for the Yanomami and displaced Venezuelans, but outcomes were incomplete, unequal and difficult to attribute causally within a one-year period;
